prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its physiological actions and its active peptide form, which enabled a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B035 as a single prize part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific case, which is a continuous chain from hormone physiology (the incretin effect and GLP-1 secretion, proglucagon processing and receptor biology, the truncated active GLP-1(7-36) peptide) to agonists with replicated randomised evidence on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism has been confirmed independently for decades, so maturity is not in question. Unanimity among our openings is not the reason I hold the position. What I tested in this round was whether any alternative configuration, a different third name or a second prize part, gives a better-supported allocation of credit, and I conclude it does not. The central satiety actions of GLP-1 also give the discovery a neural-circuit dimension, but that is a reason for interest and not a basis for credit.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakest point, and the chair's first question is the right one. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form, relative to Habener and colleagues outside the credited list, is contested, and I still cannot resolve it from the record supplied to me. Knudsen's acylated analogues are what made the biology a usable drug, so a discovery-centred citation can be read as leaving out the step that delivered patient benefit. The three-person cap forces an allocation that someone can reasonably call arbitrary. If the committee's documentary check showed that Mojsov's contribution is substantially secondary to earlier work by others, I would accept replacing her with Knudsen and recasting the citation around the therapeutic step. I would not drop Holst, whose physiology underlies the whole chain. Long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment are still accruing, though they do not touch the discovery itself.

responses.point: Perlmann worries that three seats may be too few if discovery and drug development are one indivisible achievement, and that Knudsen's industrial role is essential to the durable drug. He also asks whether a two-part prize is feasible when B035 already uses all three names.
responses.response: On the cap I agree with his arithmetic: B035 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov leaves no names for a second part, so any two-part configuration means shrinking B035 to two people, which would drop either the physiology or the active-peptide step. I do not think the evidence justifies that. On the indivisibility point I partly disagree. The prize criterion concerns the discovery, and the discovery chain is separable from the pharmacological optimisation that followed it, which can be recognised in the narrative without a seat. I do share his concern about the Mojsov record. My position is therefore that the check should be done before the vote, not that the framing should change.

responses.point: Sandberg would accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov if Mojsov's priority proves weaker than assumed, and he raises the risk that the prize reads as rewarding a commercially prominent drug class rather than physiology.
responses.response: I accept the conditional but would set the bar high. A contested priority claim is a reason to check the record, and only a finding that her contribution was derivative should change the third name. If the committee did substitute Knudsen, the citation would have to move toward the therapeutic step and the framing risk Sandberg names would become the dominant issue, so the swap is not neutral. In the absence of such a finding, Mojsov's identification of the active form is a distinct step that neither Holst's physiology nor Drucker's receptor work supplies, and I keep her in. I also take his point on commercial prominence as a reason to keep the citation worded around the hormone and its actions.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asks that if Knudsen is included the cost should fall on Mojsov rather than Holst, and he notes that his recollection of the priority history is from memory and not verified against the candidate evidence.
responses.response: I agree on the order of sacrifice: Holst's characterisation of GLP-1 secretion and the incretin effect is the physiological foundation and I would not trade it for any other name. I also share his caution about unverified recollection, since I am in the same position. None of us should settle Mojsov versus Habener from memory. If that check cannot be completed before the ballot, the evidence available to us supports the existing trio, and I would vote that way while recording that this is the least secure attribution in the configuration.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius is reluctant to drop Rosenberg from B029 because adoptive transfer of gene-engineered T cells belongs to the same lineage, and she raises Eshhar's original CAR concept as outside the credited list. She also holds B002 as an alternative and discloses her rheumatology proximity.
responses.response: I take the lineage argument seriously, but I think it shows why B029 is the harder configuration. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and the engineering of the receptor are connected in practice yet distinct in concept. With Eshhar absent as well, a trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg credits a clinical lineage with an incomplete origin, while June and Sadelain alone credit the engineered-receptor therapy but lose the lineage. Neither is as clean as B035. I therefore keep B029 as my first alternative and not as a second part. Her disclosure on B002 is handled properly by the transparency she has already given, and I would give her view on the rheumatology literature weight without treating it as a conflict.

responses.point: Linnarsson sees B046 as a mature, tool-defining discovery with Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann as a workable trio, while noting that a prize for a method may be weighed differently from a disease mechanism.
responses.response: I shared that trio in round 1, but after the exchange I am less confident in it. Every member who commented says that Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenböck have strong claims, and the channelrhodopsin discovery and its use for neuronal control are different steps, so any three names settle a credit dispute by cutting. My field uses the method daily, which is a reason for caution and not for advocacy. I keep B046 as the second alternative. I would not move it above B029, where the main attribution gap is a single missing originator.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, relative to Habener and colleagues, is secure enough to hold her place among three. I could not resolve this from the supplied record, and no one in round 1 reported verifying it.
Whether the committee will frame B035 around physiology and the active peptide or around the therapeutic step, since the second framing would require Knudsen to displace an academic discoverer.
Whether B029 can be defended with June and Sadelain alone, given that Eshhar's early CAR concept and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer are both outside that pair.
How optogenetics (B046) should be weighed as a research tool against a clinical discovery when six credited names must be cut to three.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B035, B029 or B046. My documented connections (a 2019 synthesis with Sten Grillner, collaborations with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) concern motor-circuit and stem-cell work and involve no credited name on the shortlist. Optogenetics is a method used in my field, but I have no documented tie to its credited individuals. Wahren-Herlenius's disclosure on B002 does not change my own position, since I do not prefer B002.
